papers.title: Sensory experience-induced plasticity of somatostatin interneurons occurs through two-pore potassium (K2P) channels
papers.abstract: GABAergic interneurons (INs) are powerful modulators of plasticity and learning in cortical networks, but plasticity of INs themselves is not well understood. We studied experience-dependent plasticity in somatostatin (SST) INs, which critically regulate dendritic integration, sensory tuning, and plasticity in pyramidal neurons in sensory cortex. Whether SST INs exhibit experience-dependent plasticity, and by what mechanisms, is unknown. We found that 3 days of whisker deprivation strongly downregulated intrinsic excitability of SST INs in L2/3 of somatosensory cortex, by reducing input resistance. Deprivation also increased mEPSCs onto SST INs. The reduction in intrinsic excitability was caused by an increase in leak potassium current through two-pore K+ (K2P) channels, without changes in HCN, KV1, or KV7 currents, which contribute to plasticity in other IN types and brain areas. Immunohistochemistry showed an increase in TRESK, but not other K2P channels, indicating a novel role for K2P channels in experience-dependent plasticity of interneuron excitability.

papers.title: Electrophysiological Dynamics of Default Network Suppression
papers.abstract: Distributed brain networks compete with one another in the service of information processing. One dramatic example is antagonism between networks that support internally directed cognition, often collectively referred to as the default network, and networks that orient to external events and drive action. Here we combined within-individual precision functional neuroimaging and intracranial electrophysiology to investigate network competition at high spatiotemporal resolution. In six patients, robust antagonism between networks was established during a target detection task. Network-assigned electrophysiological recordings displayed concordant responses, including in single-neuron firing rates, and further revealed the temporal dynamics of network competition. Networks involved in salience detection and action planning showed early, transient responses that peaked near the participant response. Default network suppression occurred later, reflected in decreases in high-frequency broadband activity and in single-neuron firing rates in response to targets. Examining subcortical regions revealed rapid activity increases in the thalamus and posterior hippocampus aligned to the participant response. Critically, a late evolving, sustained suppression was observed throughout the hippocampus. These findings suggest that, across cortical and subcortical regions, network competition is temporally layered. Furthermore, the hippocampus can be dissociated along its long axis during competition. Such push-pull antagonism may be fundamental to advanced human cognition, and its disruption may underlie mental illness.

papers.title: Linking Covariates to State Durations in Dynamic Brain Networks via Hidden Semi-Markov Models
papers.abstract: Hidden semi-Markov models (HSMMs) provide a flexible framework for studying dynamic functional connectivity because they represent brain activity as transitions between latent network states with explicit dwell time distributions. Although dwell times are often associated with behavioral and demographic variables, these associations are typically assessed only after model fitting using indirect group comparisons, limiting formal covariate modeling and the simultaneous inclusion of multiple predictors. In this work, we extend the HSMM framework by introducing covariate-dependent dwell time distributions through a regression-based formulation, allowing expected state duration to vary with subject-level covariates and enabling direct inference on how these factors relate to state persistence. Model parameters are estimated with an expectation-maximization algorithm, and uncertainty in the dwell-time regression coefficients is quantified using a subject-level nonparametric bootstrap. In simulations, the proposed model accurately recovered covariate effects under both shifted-Poisson and Gamma dwell time specifications, with low bias and variability. We applied the method to resting-state fMRI data from 1,000 UK Biobank participants and found that age and sex were associated with dwell times in a subset of brain states. Together, these results show that modeling dwell-time behavior directly provides a more flexible framework for studying individual differences in brain dynamics, revealing not only which states occur, but also how long individuals remain in them.

papers.title: A caudate-centered network for alexithymia derived from patients with brain tumors
papers.abstract: Alexithymia is a trait characterized by impaired emotional awareness. Previous accounts examining the neurobiological underpinnings of this trait have centered on a variety of structures, and alexithymia-causing lesions occur in disparate locations. We use lesion network mapping to derive a neural circuit for alexithymia. In a neurosurgical cohort of 45 patients with gliomas (19 female; aged 18-75 years), we compute each lesion's connectivity to the rest of the brain using a normative connectome (n = 1,000) and relate these connectivity maps to preoperative Toronto Alexithymia Scale scores using permutation testing. Lesions associated with higher alexithymia are connected to a common network that includes the bilateral caudate heads (right greater than left) and the anterior cingulate cortex, peaking in the right caudate head (family-wise error-corrected p < 0.05). The network converges with coordinates from an independent meta-analysis of gray matter volume in alexithymia (13 of 14 coordinates positive; p = 0.0004). Of the three subscales, difficulty identifying feelings localized to this network. Within the striatum, the network spans the executive and limbic subdivisions. These findings suggest a caudate-centered circuit, at the interface of affective and executive systems, that unifies disparate lesion locations.

papers.title: Comparing apples to oranges from photoreceptors to inferior temporal cortex through neural manifolds
papers.abstract: In the neural processing of color, cone photoreceptor outputs are combined over successive stages to form inferior temporal cortex (IT) cells with narrower color tuning and more diverse peak preferences. To understand the benefits of these transformations, we explored the capability of photoreceptor, retinal ganglion cell and IT population responses to distinguish between pairs of natural fruits and vegetables, based solely on their color distributions extracted from hyperspectral images. Simulations with realistic Poisson response variability show that linear separations are possible for many more pairs by IT neurons. Shapes of low-dimensional manifolds extracted from neural population responses explain the improvement.

papers.title: Variable errors suppress implicit motor adaptation among older adults
papers.abstract: Age-related changes in motor control networks manifest in a highly task-dependent manner. Although older adults can display enhanced implicit sensorimotor adaptation, this effect is inconsistent across perturbation types (e.g., visuomotor vs. force-field perturbations). Because these perturbations induce different errors to drive learning, their distinct effects on learning suggest that specific properties of the error signal modulate the extent of adaptation among older adults. Here, we investigated whether age-related hyper-adaptation is modulated by error variability. More specifically, we manipulated the consistency of error direction during an error-clamp visuomotor adaptation task in both younger and older adults. While consistent errors elicited enhanced implicit adaptation in older adults relative to younger controls, variable errors did not. These findings reveal that error consistency is a critical prerequisite for age-related enhancements in implicit motor learning. Rather than exhibiting unconstrained hyper-adaptation, older adults maintain an adaptive error-sensitivity mechanism that prevents hyper-recruitment of implicit systems in noisy motor environments.

papers.title: Allele-selective knockdown of mutant DNAJB6 improves molecular features in a primary mouse myotube model of LGMDD1
papers.abstract: Dominant variants in DNAJB6 cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy D1 (LGMDD1), a progressive myopathy associated with disrupted protein homeostasis. Because complete loss of DNAJB6 is embryonic lethal in mice, we evaluated allele-selective knockdown as a strategy to reduce mutant DNAJB6 while preserving wild-type protein. We generated a knock-in mouse carrying an N-terminal 3xFLAG tag on the wild-type Dnajb6 allele, allowing endogenous wild-type and F90I DNAJB6, the murine equivalent of human F89I, to be measured within the same sample. Flag-LGMDD1 mice recapitulated the functional, myopathological, and biochemical features seen in other LGMDD1 models and in human disease. F90I DNAJB6 was more abundant and degraded more slowly than wild-type DNAJB6, and LGMDD1 muscle and primary myotubes showed altered protein handling at baseline and following proteostatic stress. Comparative proteomic analyses identified DNAJA4 as a candidate marker responsive to pathogenic DNAJB6 activity. A two-stage mismatch screen identified a lead candidate siRNA with 264-fold selectivity for F90I DNAJB6. In primary Flag-LGMDD1 myotubes, this siRNA selectively reduced F90I DNAJB6 and shifted several baseline and stress-dependent molecular abnormalities involving p62, HSP70, DNAJA4, and markers associated with unfolded protein response signaling toward control values. These findings establish cellular proof of concept for allele-selective knockdown in LGMDD1.

papers.title: Allele-agnostic KCNH1 suppression rescues gain-of-function developmental epileptic encephalopathy
papers.abstract: Gain-of-function variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1, cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) characterized by seizures, developmental delay and intellectual disability. While pathogenic variants enhance channel activity, loss of KCNH1 is tolerated in humans and mice, suggesting that allele-agnostic gene suppression may represent a viable therapeutic strategy. Here, we developed a gapmer antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting KCNH1 and evaluated its efficacy in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and a knock-in mouse model of KCNH1-related disorder. Neurons carrying the pathogenic KCNH1 variants I494V or G375R exhibited a shared phenotype characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential and abnormalities in neuronal network activity despite largely preserved intrinsic firing properties. ASOs efficiently reduced KCNH1 expression without disrupting network activity in control neurons. In contrast, ASO treatment normalized network dysfunction across both mutant genotypes, demonstrating that distinct KCNH1 gain-of-function variants converge on a reversible disease state. To assess the efficacy of ASOs in vivo, we generated a new Kcnh1-R357Q knock-in mouse model that exhibited profound seizures and early mortality. A single ASO treatment reduced seizure burden significantly and restored survival to near-normal levels. Together, these findings establish KCNH1 suppression as a precision therapeutic strategy for KCNH1-related DEEs and provide a framework for treating gain-of-function epilepsies in which partial gene reduction is clinically tolerated.

papers.title: Identifying a neurochemical signature of the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus that predicts individual variability in cue-reward learning
papers.abstract: To investigate neurochemical factors that may confer vulnerability to psychiatric disorders, we used an animal model that captures a transdiagnostically relevant neurobehavioral endophenotype. During a Pavlovian conditioned approach paradigm, rats learn the predictive relationship between a lever cue and food reward. A subset of rats, sign trackers, also attribute incentive motivational value to the lever cue. Relative to non sign trackers, STs are more impulsive, have attentional deficits, and show greater reinstatement of drug seeking behavior. The paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus is a key neural node implicated in these individual differences. We combined in vivo microdialysis with liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry to quantify 22 neurobiologically relevant small molecules in the PVT before and 24 hours after Pavlovian training. Before training, glucose concentrations in the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus were higher in rats subsequently classified as sign trackers than in non sign trackers and were correlated with the Pavlovian conditioned approach index used to phenotype the rats. Glucose concentrations decreased after training, and the magnitude of change differed between phenotypes. Multivariate regression identified baseline neurochemical profiles in the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus associated with subsequent Pavlovian conditioned approach behavior. These findings identify a candidate PVT neurochemical signature that precedes behavioral phenotyping and may mark the propensity to sign track, providing insight into potential mechanisms underlying vulnerability to psychiatric disorders characterized by maladaptive cue motivated behavior.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction is Part of a Novel Mechanism for Chemotherapy-Induced Neuropathic Pain
papers.abstract: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a common, persistent complication of cancer treatment, yet the mechanisms sustaining pain remain unclear. Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in chronic pain, but its role in spinal cord dysfunction after chemotherapy, and whether it can be reversed, is unknown. Here, we show that paclitaxel-induced persistent mechanical allodynia was associated with spinal cord (L1-L6) mitochondrial dysfunction 18 days after the last injection, including reduced oxygen consumption and membrane potential ({Psi}m) in the non-phosphorylated state, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and electron transfer capacity. Paclitaxel also increased susceptibility to mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP)-induction, lowering calcium retention capacity at 3, 8, and 13 days after the last injection. Acute ex-vivo paclitaxel exposure had a similar effect, and cyclosporin A, an mPTP blocker, significantly reversed it. Consistent with a causal role for mitochondrial impairment, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT), initiated after allodynia developed, improved oxygen consumption and {Psi}m and progressively enhanced mechanical thresholds. Likewise, intrathecal delivery of healthy mitochondria to the spinal cord attenuated established allodynia in paclitaxel-treated rats and reduced mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity in other pain models, sciatic nerve crush and capsaicin. These findings identify persistent spinal mitochondrial dysfunction and increased mPTP susceptibility as features of CIPN and support mitochondrial protection as a therapeutic strategy for CIPN and other pain conditions.

papers.title: Ergodic breakdown of brain dynamics under chronnectome complexity across cognitive states and age
papers.abstract: Chronnectome complexity, the extent to which time-varying functional connectivity follows a structured sequence of distinct configurations, contributes to shaping large-scale brain dynamics. However, it remains unclear how this complexity influences the encoding of information that distinguishes resting state and task conditions. In ergodic theory, time averages represent ensemble behavior under ergodicity, which breaks down when dynamics are non-stationary, as when activity moves sequentially between distinct regimes. We hypothesize that this information resides in time-averaged connectivity under lower-complexity conditions but in trajectory geometry under higher-complexity conditions, where brain activity traverses distinct configurations over time, consistent with ergodic breakdown, which we term the textit{information migration principle}. We formulate this as dynamics-driven multi-class classification and introduce the Brain Dynamics Classifier (BDC), an interpretable data-driven mechanistic model in which a graph neural network embeds dynamic functional connectivity into a latent space and a neural ordinary differential equation learns the vector field governing trajectories through that space. The proposed model derives two complementary representations within a single learned dynamical system, capturing time-averaged connectivity, which is sufficient under ergodic dynamics, and trajectory geometry, which preserves the temporal organization obscured by averaging under non-ergodic dynamics. Our results show high classification accuracy, $97.4%$ for eight conditions in the Human Connectome Project young adult cohort and $92.2%$ for four in the aging cohort. To test the information migration principle, we ablated the time-averaged representation and found that trajectory contributions varied with chronnectome complexity, from high for Working Memory to absent for Relational Reasoning, consistent with ergodic breakdown. Including subcortical regions further increased trajectory contributions for affective conditions. In aging, the distinction between higher and lower complexity conditions was preserved, resting-state dynamics became less ergodic with advancing age, and higher fluid intelligence was associated with more ergodic resting-state dynamics.

papers.title: A Neurocompliant Ionic Conductive Hydrogel Orchestrates Glial and Vascular Remodeling to Mitigate Traumatic Brain Injury
papers.abstract: Developing conductive scaffolds for neural regeneration is often hindered by the cytotoxicity and mechanical mismatch inherent to conventional electronic fillers. Here, we report an ultrasoft ionically conductive hydrogel engineered by grafting choline-based bioionic liquids (BIL) onto fish gelatin (FiBGel). Systematic optimization yields brain-mimetic conductivity (0.25-0.68 S/m), elastic moduli (0.6-0.9 kPa), and physiological water content (72-81%). In 3D culture, the matrix drives spontaneous neurogenesis, achieving ~90% MAP2+ neurons with robust calcium signaling, while concurrently supporting endothelial network formation. We report the first intracerebral administration of a BIL hydrogel, demonstrating remarkable biocompatibility and immunomodulation. In a traumatic brain injury model, a single FiBGel dose halves reactive astrogliosis, enhances cortical revascularization, and limits lesion cavity expansion. Leveraging an FDA-recognized micronutrient, FiBGel offers a translatable strategy that integrates neuromechanics, conductivity, immune modulation, and vascular support within one injectable scaffold for minimally invasive treatment of brain injuries.

papers.title: Mapping and longitudinal imaging of potentiated synapses in the mouse hippocampus using SynActive-eGRASP
papers.abstract: Identifying individual synapses that undergo long-term potentiation following learning at specific circuits remains a major challenge in neuroscience. To address this problem, we developed SA-eGRASP, a genetically encoded reporter that combines SynActive (SA) targeting with enhanced GFP Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners (eGRASP). SA drives the expression of the postsynaptic half of eGRASP at potentiated spines via the 5' and 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of the immediate-early gene Arc, thus enabling selective labeling of individual synapses that are both structurally connected and have undergone potentiation through transsynaptic GFP reconstitution. Here, we validated SA-eGRASP and combined it with high-resolution optical imaging to generate a detailed map of hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapses subjected to potentiation following contextual fear conditioning in mice. The high signal-to-noise ratio of SA-eGRASP, allowed us to track individual potentiated dendritic spines over the course of several days, to investigate the long-term dynamics of CA3-CA1 potentiated dendritic spines, and to study the selective potentiation of a subset of spines upon experience. SA-eGRASP paves the way to the investigation of synaptic engrams by enabling longitudinal, circuit-specific investigation of synapses potentiated during learning in mice performing naturalistic behaviors.

papers.title: Distinguishing evidence accumulation from choice confidence in neural signatures of perceptual decision making
papers.abstract: Human electrophysiology research has identified the centro-parietal positivity (CPP) as an apparent neural correlate of sensory evidence accumulation during perceptual decision-making. The CPP has also been shown to closely scale with subjective confidence. Coupled with the fact of its domain-generality and lack of choice selectivity, this observation raises the possibility that the CPP might in fact trace subjective confidence rather than cumulative evidence, two quantities that are closely correlated in most experiments. To disentangle confidence from cumulative evidence, we used predictive cues with 80% validity to manipulate prior expectations of participants during a contrast discrimination task while recording electroencephalography (EEG). At the time of decision termination, confidence is expected to reach a higher level for validly cued versus invalidly cued choices, whereas the opposite would be expected of a cumulative evidence signal due to biased decision starting points. As expected, valid cues led to faster, more accurate and more confident responses compared to invalid and neutral cues. At the neural level, cues produced systematic increases in preparation of the expected action prior to evidence onset as indexed by premotor mu/beta activity, consistent with cue-biased criterion adjustments. The pre-response CPP amplitude was significantly reduced for validly cued choices and the effect remained even when matching for confidence. Together these findings suggest that the CPP is not a direct read-out of subjective confidence, but an evidence accumulation signal that contributes to both decision formation and confidence estimation.

papers.title: Changes in anterior cingulate connectivity associated with response to antidepressant treatment for major depressive disorder
papers.abstract: Background: Resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) involving the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the hippocampal formation has been implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD) and antidepressant response. However, it remains unclear whether connectivity changes in distinct ACC subdivisions and hippocampal formation reflect general antidepressant effects or are specifically associated with clinical improvement. Methods: Forty-one, unmedicated adults with MDD underwent functional MRI before and after 8 weeks of sertraline or bupropion treatment. Seed-based rsFC analyses examined subgenual ACC (sgACC), pregenual ACC (pgACC), dorsal ACC (dACC), and hippocampal formation connectivity. Linear mixed-effects models tested whether connectivity change was associated with treatment response, remission, and dimensional improvement in depressive symptoms. Results: Thirty individuals (73.2%) responded to treatment and 26 (63.4%) achieved remission. Overall, rsFC decreased pre- to post-treatment between (1) dACC and pgACC (but not sgACC and hippocampal formation) and (2) cortical regions primarily involving default mode and frontoparietal networks. When considering treatment response, differences in sgACC and pgACC connectivity with temporal and inferior frontal regions emerged (increased in responders vs. decreased in non-responders). Remission was similarly associated with increased sgACC connectivity with temporal and prefrontal regions, and increased sgACC connectivity with temporal cortical regions related to greater reductions in depressive symptoms. Conclusions: Antidepressant treatment was associated with distinct patterns of ACC connectivity change, with general reductions in dorsal and pregenual connectivity but increases in subgenual and pregenual connectivity associated with favorable clinical outcomes. Findings suggest that changes in sgACC/pgACC connectivity are particularly relevant to antidepressant treatment response. Keywords: Major depressive disorder; Resting-state functional connectivity; Anterior cingulate cortex; Antidepressant treatment; Treatment response; Subgenual anterior cingulate cortex.

papers.title: Targeting distinct neuronal populations with AAV vectors reveals neurogenesis-associated anxiolytic effects of JNK inhibition
papers.abstract: c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) regulates stress responses and affective behaviour, but the neural populations mediating these effects remain unclear. Here, we delivered a nucleus-targeted JNK inhibitor to the mouse brain using blood-brain barrier-crossing adeno-associated virus vectors with distinct cellular tropisms. JNK inhibition produced strikingly different behavioural outcomes depending on the neuronal populations targeted. Only AAV-PHP.eB-hSyn1-mediated delivery reproduced the previously reported anxiolytic phenotype, whereas AAV.CAP-B10-hSyn1 increased locomotor activity and depressive-like behaviour and AAV.CAP-B10-mDlx reduced locomotion while enhancing object recognition memory. The anxiolytic response was accompanied by reduced hilar mossy cell abundance and an approximately two-fold increase in doublecortin-positive newborn granule neurons in the dentate gyrus. Notably, this phenotype mirrors our previous findings following selective JNK inhibition in adult hippocampal progenitor cells, implicating the neurogenic niche as a convergent substrate for anxiolytic responses to JNK inhibition. Proteomic analysis of plasma extracellular vesicles revealed widespread alterations in metabolic and inflammatory proteins upon JNK inhibition, despite neuron-restricted transgene expression. Together, these findings demonstrate that the behavioural and systemic consequences of JNK inhibition depend critically on the neural populations targeted and identify hippocampal neurogenesis-associated circuits involving mossy cells as candidate mediators of JNK-dependent anxiety regulation.

papers.title: An anatomical and day-night atlas links cochlear immunity to adjacent bone marrow
papers.abstract: The cochlea lies within marrow-bearing bone. How this neighbouring marrow relates to cochlear immunity and daily physiology remains poorly resolved. We profiled 160,643 cells from mouse cochlea and adjacent temporal-bone marrow at six times of day, with rhythm inference calibrated for one pooled sample per time. Three-dimensional confocal reconstruction mapped vascular connections between marrow and cochlea and localized neutrophils along this interface. Neutrophils also occupied healthy cochlear fluids. Parabiosis findings were consistent with a local marrow contribution to cochlear immunity. Structural cochlear cells maintained synchronized, light-entrained clocks. Cochlear neutrophil programmes aligned with circulating neutrophils and opposed those in marrow, with independent flow cytometry supporting daily changes in immune composition and CXCR4. A shared night-associated heat-shock programme was attenuated after noise in an independent cohort. These anatomical and temporal data provide a reference for testing local marrow supply and the origins of cochlear immune rhythms.

papers.title: Quantifying Excitation-Inhibition Harmony and Its Breakdown during Epileptogenesis in a Spiking Neural Network of the Hippocampal CA1
papers.abstract: Epileptogenesis is often linked to disruptions in excitation-inhibition (E-I) balance, yet its quantitative characterization remains limited. Understanding and quantifying this E-I balance could enable earlier diagnosis and targeted treatment of epilepsy. We investigate competitive E-I harmony and its breakdown using a biologically grounded spiking neural network model of hippocampal CA1 that incorporates two structural pathological mechanisms: pyramidal cell (PC) axonal sprouting and loss of inhibitory interneurons. As recurrent excitatory connectivity increases via PC axonal sprouting or inhibitory interneuron populations decline through interneuron loss, the network undergoes sequential transitions from a healthy phase (HP) to an interictal pathological phase (IIP) and finally to an ictal pathological phase (IP). At the input level, we introduce the competition degree, Cd (= SE / SI), as the ratio of the strengths of excitatory (SE) to inhibitory (SI) synaptic inputs to PCs, to quantify their competitive E-I harmony. As an input-side indicator, Cd remains near 2.6 in HP, exhibits a discontinuous, abrupt jump to ~ 60 at the HP [->] IIP transition and rises further thereafter. At the output level, the corresponding output-side measure, the population-averaged mean firing rate (MFR) of PCs, , also exhibits a discontinuous, abrupt jump from ~ 4 to ~ 200 Hz at the HP [->] IIP transition and rises further thereafter, indicating progressive pathological hyperexcitability. Together, these results establish a cause-and-effect framework linking the input-side indicator Cd (cause) to the output-side measure (effect). Accordingly, Cd may serve as a potential quantitative biomarker of competitive E-I harmony and its breakdown, providing a computational causal framework that links structural pathological mechanisms to epileptogenic state transitions and offering potential for translation into diagnostic tools and therapeutic applications.

papers.title: Replicable Connectivity and Spectral Alterations of Functional Networks in Major Depression
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is usually characterized in functional MRI through connectivity alone, often in samples too small to resolve its modest effects. Here we applied multi-scale, template-guided independent component analysis to resting-state data from the multi-site MDD-DIRECT cohort and jointly examined the connectivity, spectral content and spatial composition of 105 intrinsic brain networks. Differences between patients and controls were widespread, small and structured: cerebello-subcortical coupling was reduced, subcortical--somatomotor coupling was increased, and spectral power shifted from lower to higher frequencies, most prominently in the thalamus, which also showed the most altered connectivity. Spatial composition differed in every network examined. In a smaller independent cohort, the direction of effect agreed for 95% of significant connections, 78% of significant spectral effects and 77% of the largest spatial-composition effects. Depression therefore alters several distinct properties of intrinsic networks, consistently across cohorts and most prominently in the thalamus.

papers.title: Midbrain neurons regulate the production of courtship squeaks in female mice
papers.abstract: Animals produce different vocalization types (e.g., contact calls, mating calls) to communicate in different behavioral contexts, but how the brain is organized to enable the production of different vocalization types remains poorly understood. Recent work found that specialized neurons in the midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) regulate the production of ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) in female and male mice, but these PAG-USV neurons are not required for the production of broadband vocalizations (squeaks). To identify PAG neurons that may regulate the production of squeaks, we used an activity-dependent labeling strategy (TRAP2) to identify and manipulate PAG neurons that are active in association with the production of courtship squeaks in female mice. Optogenetic activation of courtship squeak-TRAPed PAG neurons elicits the production of squeaks, while ablation of TRAPed PAG neurons blocks the production of courtship squeaks without altering female non-vocal courtship behaviors. Surprisingly, ablation of courtship squeak-TRAPed PAG neurons did not affect the production of footshock-elicited squeaks. Moreover, non-selective PAG ablation, which blocked the production of courtship squeaks in females and USVs in both sexes, attenuated but did not block the production of footshock-elicited squeaks. Our results identify a population of PAG neurons that critically regulates the production of courtship squeaks in female mice and also suggest that a non-canonical, PAG-independent pathway regulates the production of pain-elicited vocalizations.

papers.title: First-in-class -PET radiotracers for GPR39: A platform for noninvasive target engagement imaging in vivo
papers.abstract: Disrupted zinc homeostasis is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. As a key zinc-sensing receptor, GPR39, a G protein-coupled receptor implicated in neurodegeneration, vascular regulation, and neuropsychiatric disorders, represents an emerging target for molecular imaging. However, the lack of suitable positron emission tomography (PET) radiotracers has limited the in vivo characterization of GPR39. Quantitative assessment of GPR39 in vivo could improve our understanding of its role in physiology and disease and facilitate the development and evaluation of targeted therapeutics. Here, we introduce [18F]GPR39 2.1 as a PET radiotracer for specific imaging of GPR39. [18F]GPR39 2.1 exhibited excellent serum stability with negligible radiometabolite formation. In vitro cell uptake studies demonstrated a 55-70% reduction in tracer uptake following pharmacological blockade. PET imaging showed rapid brain uptake, efficient blood-brain barrier penetration, and gradual washout. Blockade studies in rats demonstrated significant reductions in brain uptake of up to approximately 90% (p<0.0001) across multiple brain regions. GPR39 specificity was further validated in GPR39 knockout mice, which showed 76% (p<0.002) and 90% (p<0.0002) reductions in brain uptake by PET imaging and biodistribution, respectively. Moreover, 5xFAD transgenic mice exhibited significantly lower brain uptake by PET imaging (40%, p<0.0002) and biodistribution (77%, p<0.002), indicating sensitivity of [18F]GPR39 2.1 to disease-associated alterations in GPR39. Biodistribution studies demonstrated favorable pharmacokinetics, while autoradiography further confirmed GPR39-specific binding, consistent with the PET and biodistribution findings. Collectively, these results establish [18F]GPR39 2.1 as a stable, brain-penetrant, and highly specific PET radiotracer for noninvasive imaging of GPR39 in vivo. This work provides a translational framework for investigating GPR39 biology and supports the development of GPR39 as an imaging and therapeutic target in neurological and systemic diseases associated with GPR39 dysregulation.

papers.title: Human medial frontal neurons represent integrated semantic content and sensory evidence to inform decision-making
papers.abstract: Humans can reconfigure how they act on the world from a single verbal instruction. Central to this capacity is the ability to represent what an instruction specifies and to bring that content to bear on incoming sensory evidence. However, little is known about where in the human brain instruction content is encoded, how it combines with sensory evidence to produce a choice, and how this integration relates to behavior. Here, we characterized single-neuron and population responses recorded in the ventral temporal cortex, medial temporal lobe, medial frontal cortex and ventromedial prefrontal cortex of neurosurgical patients performing a verbal instruction task. On each trial, a written instruction specified which stimulus feature was relevant and whether the correct response was to choose or to reject the stimulus that best matched it, so that the same image pair required opposite responses under different instructions. Only medial frontal populations jointly encoded the instructed task, and the target feature, whereas ventral temporal populations encoded stimulus features along axes that generalized across instruction conditions. Choice representation emerged first in ventromedial prefrontal and then in medial frontal cortex during stimulus presentation, before a motor response could be prepared. Shuffling instruction content selectively degraded prediction of medial frontal population activity, whereas shuffling stimulus identity selectively degraded ventral temporal activity. To ask how these representations could be computed, we trained a vision-language model with separable visual and linguistic streams converging on a recurrent decision module to perform the same task. Its visual embeddings predicted held-out ventral temporal activity and its recurrent activations revealed a task solution space that predicted medial frontal activity, and the strength of this alignment tracked behavioral accuracy. These results identify a cortical hierarchy in which medial frontal circuitry represents the content of verbal goals and acts on a ventral temporal substrate whose representational axes remain stable, and indicate that functional hierarchies discovered in artificial networks can serve as predictive models of human neural circuitry.

papers.title: Pre-synaptic facilitation of corticospinal output improves dexterity and finemotor control after stroke
papers.abstract: The corticospinal tract (CST) is a neural pathway that supports skilled use of the arm and hand. Lesions of corticospinal axons result in muscle weakness, deficits of gross motor function, and loss of proximal and distal dexterous control for which effective treatments are still lacking. Here we exploited excitatory connections from motor thalamus to primary motor cortex to potentiate surviving descending signals and restore volitional arm and hand control in three monkeys with corticospinal tract lesion, using deep brain stimulation. Stimulation targeted to thalamocortical projections facilitated upper-limb movements, enabling monkeys with arm and hand paralysis to perform unconstrained 3D reach and fine dexterous tasks. Stimulation improved strength, hand gross motor function, and digits control. Electrophysiology suggested that effects were mediated by and more effective when targeting fibers with monosynaptic connection to the corticospinal motoneurons. Stimulation was delivered in continuous with FDA-clinically approved parameters holding realistic promises of clinical translation.

papers.title: Bayesian Modeling of Context-Specific Goal-Directed and Habitual Control in Sequential Decision Making
papers.abstract: It is an open question how context-specific habits develop alongside goal-directed planning. We examined action sequence repetition, contingency change, and context switching using a three-step optimization task with interleaved planning and habit contexts. During an initial acquisition phase, optimal sequences varied in the planning context but remained constant in the habit context. When contingencies changed, the original habit sequence became suboptimal and another became optimal. Action sequence repetition improved response speed and optimal-choice performance in the habit context relative to the planning context. Following the contingency change, both advantages initially reversed. Optimal-choice performance in the habit context subsequently recovered but did not significantly exceed that in the planning context, while responses remained slower in the habit context. Context switches reduced optimal-choice performance in both directions, with additional slowing when switching from habit to planning. The Bayesian contextual control model captured choice patterns through learned action sequence priors, goal-directed evaluation, and context inference. Allowing a context-stability bias to vary across participants did not improve model performance. These findings suggest that sequence repetition facilitates performance under stable contingencies while impairing adaptation to change.

papers.title: A Common Recognition Architecture Across Memory Scales
papers.abstract: Recognition decisions occur across memory episodes that vary vastly in scale, from compact single-item episodes to extended experiences involving hundreds of items. To test how memory scale shapes the neural mechanisms underlying old/new judgments, we recorded EEG while participants performed a recognition memory task across set sizes ranging from 1 to 128 items (spanning 2 to 256 recognition judgments). Classic electrophysiological signatures of recognition, including frontal and parietal old/new effects, persisted continuously across set sizes. Furthermore, multivariate neural classifiers trained on small memory scales generalized robustly across set sizes. Rather than revealing distinct neural formats, increasing memory scale produced systematic, continuous shifts in the timing and strength of a shared recognition response: signals emerged progressively later and weaker at larger memory scales. Temporal-alignment and cross-correlation analyses demonstrated that responses across scales followed a common waveform trajectory, with timing shifts propagating into motor response preparation. Finally, individual difference analyses revealed that this common recognition format exhibits scale-dependent behavioral relevance, tracking working-memory capacity at smaller scales and long-term memory performance at larger scales. Together, these findings demonstrate that recognition signals share a common neural format across scale while changing dynamically in timing, strength, and behavioral relevance, providing evidence for convergence onto a shared recognition architecture.

papers.title: Visual capture of the head-direction signal in a rat model of Fragile X Syndrome
papers.abstract: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is a common inherited monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability (ASD/ID), conditions frequently associated with altered sensory processing and multisensory integration. However, the circuit mechanisms underlying these alterations remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the integration of visual and self-motion information in the head-direction (HD) system in a rat model of FXS (Fmr1-/y rats). Using high-density silicon probes, we recorded neuronal activity in the postsubiculum (PoSub), a cortical hub of the HD system, while adult Fmr1-/y and wild-type (WT) rats experienced repeated rotations of a visual landmark. In WT rats, the HD signal only partially followed landmark rotations, consistent with weighted integration of visual and self-motion information, and visual landmark control progressively weakened across repeated cue conflicts. In contrast, the HD signal in Fmr1-/y rats closely followed landmark rotations and failed to show experience-dependent recalibration. This enhanced visual capture was accompanied by reduced angular head velocity tuning in PoSub neurons, indicating weakened representation of self-motion information. Together, these findings reveal an altered balance between visual and self-motion inputs to the HD system in a rat model of FXS and identify a possible circuit-level mechanism through which sensory integration of vision and self-motion may be disrupted in ASD/ID.

papers.title: Automatic orofacial behaviors remap within cortical substrates for voluntary motor control in freely moving primates
papers.abstract: Orofacial behaviors, like yawning and emotional facial expressions, involve phylogenetically conserved subcortical circuits. Yet, their context-dependent modulation in primates suggests overlooked cortical contributions. Here, we wirelessly recorded from 640 ventral motor and premotor sites in two freely moving macaques during spontaneous orofacial actions combining automatic and voluntary components to varying degrees (yawning, threat, bite, drink). We identified coupling between synaptic input (local field potential) and spiking output in 169 spatially distributed sites during yawning, while threat display was sparsely represented. Yawn-related sites exhibited an early beta-band suppression followed by high-gamma power enhancement. Of 401 isolated single neurons, 95 (predominantly putative medium-sized pyramidal cells) encoded yawning, mostly together with voluntary biting and drinking actions. No modulation was found during the observation of yawning by conspecifics. Yawn-related units either switched or maintained their mouth opening/closing tuning across yawning and more voluntary actions, suggesting counteracting and synergistic downstream influences on yawning motor control. In contrast, threat-related units predominantly preserved their opening/closing tuning during biting and drinking. Head-free intracortical microstimulation of sites hosting yawn-related units preferentially evoked localized mouth and face movements, supporting their causal role in orofacial motor control. Finally, projecting neural activity into a low-dimensional manifold showed that voluntarily controlled and largely automatic behaviors engaged distinct population dynamics while preserving the discriminability of individual orofacial displays. These findings reveal that cortical substrates of voluntary motor control can be recruited to shape otherwise automatic orofacial displays.

papers.title: Ogg1 regulates context-dependent glial states in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Oxidative DNA damage is an early hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), but whether Ogg1, a key enzyme in oxidative DNA repair, contributes to disease pathogenesis remains unclear. Here, we show that Ogg1 exerts opposing effects under physiological and disease conditions. Ogg1 deficiency impaired memory and induced glial transcriptional alterations under physiological conditions, whereas in APP/PS1 mice it improved memory, reduced amyloid burden and attenuated AD-associated glial remodeling. These effects occurred without changes in global 8-oxo-dG levels and were accompanied by changes in chromatin accessibility and gene expression, supporting a non-canonical role for Ogg1 in transcriptional regulation. Single-nucleus transcriptomics revealed strong transcriptional responses to Ogg1 deficiency across all major glial cell types and showed that Ogg1-dependent glial transcriptional programs are strongly conserved in human AD. These findings identify Ogg1 as a context-dependent regulator of glial cell states and reveal an unexpected role in AD-associated glial remodeling.

papers.title: Transcriptomic and Metabolomic Analysis of the Caudate and Putamen in ADHD
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly heritable, heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder that typically manifests in childhood; however, transcriptomic studies have inadequately accounted for age of onset and subtype, with cohorts largely comprising of adults. To address this gap, we established a stringently phenotyped ADHD cohort (up to 19 years; clinically diagnosed combined and inattentive-type ADHD) and integrated postmortem caudate and putamen bulk RNA-seq, LC-MS metabolomics, MEGENA gene co-expression analysis, and cross-study comparison. We identified 279 up- and 35 downregulated DEGs in the caudate and 110 up- and 89 downregulated DEGs in the putamen. The combined caudate-putamen metabolomic analysis revealed dopamine dysregulation (1.68-fold reduction) and dysregulation of four additional metabolites. Enrichment analysis revealed shared molecular signatures involving immune responses, ATP metabolism and calcium ion-dependent signaling, with region-specific differences in the direction of alteration. Neuronal homeostasis, and protein stress showed suppression in the putamen, along with activation of neurotransmitter reuptake, whereas CSF circulation and ECM organization were activated in the caudate, with suppression in CNS myelination, and signs of ventricular perturbations. MEGENA identified 26 ADHD-associated caudate modules and 33 putamen modules. These modules captured canonical synaptic and neuronal-circuitry pathways alongside cellular differentiation, metabolism, and cell-survival processes. FGD1 emerged as a candidate caudate hub gene among the neuronal modules. Cross-study comparison analysis suggested that molecular alterations in ADHD may be age-dependent. Additionally, assessing levels of 76 potential risk genes identified by a large ADHD GWAS study one ARTN exhibited dysregulated levels in putamen and none in caudate. Together, these findings reveal brain-region-specific molecular dysregulation in ADHD across pathways extending beyond canonical neurotransmission to immune, differentiation, and energy-metabolic processes, along with novel evidence of perturbations in the understudied lateral ventricles.

papers.title: The mouse midbrain periaqueductal gray is organized into target-specific output populations
papers.abstract: How brains select between behaviours and coordinate their execution is a central question in neuroscience. The vertebrate periaqueductal gray (PAG) controls a remarkable range of instinctive behaviours, from escape and freezing to hunting, vocalization, and micturition. Its columnar organization, the classical framework for mapping these functions, cannot explain how one region controls so many, often mutually exclusive, behaviours. To determine how PAG output is organized, we generated a whole-brain, column- and cell-type-specific synaptic projection atlas of the mouse PAG, showing distinct dorsal and ventral outputs and dense within-PAG connectivity. Retrograde tracing from four motor-related target regions identified segregated PAG populations, biased towards, but not confined to, individual columns. Channelrhodopsin-2-assisted circuit mapping showed that one such population, projecting to the cuneiform nucleus, provides substantial local collaterals, positioned to shape ongoing PAG activity. These findings uncover a modular output architecture that extends the columnar framework, offering a circuit logic for how one brain region produces diverse behaviours.
